$comment: A second family tree, orthogonal to bedrock.json's composition tree. Composition asks 'what is X made of' (organs, cells, molecules — downward into parts). Taxonomy asks 'what IS X' (a classification by shared traits — upward into categories). Every group has exactly one parent: real taxonomic rank is a strict hierarchy, not a DAG like composition can be. Sourced from Wikipedia rather than the school-level PDFs that prompted this file, to match every other fact in this game.

groups.name: Animalia
groups.fact: Multicellular, eukaryotic, and unlike plants or fungi, gets its energy by eating other organisms rather than making its own food.

groups.name: Chordata
groups.fact: Defined by a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and paired pharyngeal slits — all present at some point in development, even in species where the adult loses them.

groups.name: Vertebrata
groups.fact: The notochord present in every chordate embryo is replaced, in this group alone, by a bony or cartilaginous vertebral column by adulthood.

groups.name: Mammalia
groups.fact: Warm-blooded, has hair or fur at some life stage, and the females produce milk from mammary glands — the trait that gives the class its name.

groups.name: Aves
groups.fact: The only living animals with feathers. Warm-blooded, lays hard-shelled eggs, and its forelimbs are modified into wings even in flightless species.

groups.name: Reptilia
groups.fact: Cold-blooded, breathes with lungs, and covered in dry, scaly skin rather than the moist skin of an amphibian. Most lay leathery or hard-shelled eggs on land.

groups.name: Amphibia
groups.fact: Cold-blooded with smooth, permeable skin used for extra gas exchange — most start life in water breathing through gills and move onto land as lungs develop.

groups.name: Ray-finned fish
groups.fact: Fins supported by bony spines (rays) rather than the fleshy lobes of a lungfish or the cartilage of a shark — about 96% of all living fish species belong here.

groups.name: Cartilaginous fish
groups.fact: A skeleton built entirely of cartilage rather than bone — sharks, rays and skates all belong here, one of the oldest still-living vertebrate lineages.

groups.name: Arthropoda
groups.fact: A segmented body in a jointed exoskeleton, which has to be moulted to grow — the largest animal phylum by far, over 80% of all described animal species.

groups.name: Insecta
groups.fact: A body in three parts — head, thorax, abdomen — six jointed legs, and usually two antennae. More described species than every other animal class combined.

groups.name: Arachnida
groups.fact: Eight legs and no antennae, unlike an insect's six legs and two antennae. Spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites all belong here.

groups.name: Malacostraca
groups.fact: The largest class of crustaceans — crabs, lobsters, shrimp and woodlice — typically with a body in a head, thorax and abdomen, and paired appendages on most segments.

groups.name: Mollusca
groups.fact: Soft-bodied, usually with a muscular foot and a mantle that in most species secretes a shell — the second-largest animal phylum after arthropods.

groups.name: Gastropoda
groups.fact: Snails and slugs — molluscs that move on a single broad foot, most with a coiled shell, though slugs have reduced or lost theirs entirely.

groups.name: Cephalopoda
groups.fact: Octopuses, squid and cuttlefish — the foot is drawn up around the head into arms or tentacles, and this is the most intelligent class of invertebrate known.

groups.name: Bivalvia
groups.fact: Mussels, oysters, clams and scallops — a shell in two hinged halves and no radula, the rasping tongue almost every other mollusc feeds with.

groups.name: Cnidaria
groups.fact: Radially symmetric, with stinging cells called cnidocytes on its tentacles — jellyfish, corals and sea anemones all belong here.

groups.name: Echinodermata
groups.fact: Exclusively marine, with a calcium-carbonate skeleton just under the skin and a water-driven vascular system used for movement — starfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers.

groups.name: Annelida
groups.fact: Segmented worms — earthworms, leeches, ragworms — the body divided into repeating rings, each usually carrying its own set of internal organs.

groups.name: Platyhelminthes
groups.fact: Flatworms — soft, unsegmented, with no body cavity and a gut (where present) with only one opening, serving as both mouth and anus.

groups.name: Porifera
groups.fact: Sponges — no true tissues, nerves or organs, just a loose aggregate of specialised cells filtering food from water pumped through the body's own pores.

groups.name: Primates
groups.fact: Forward-facing eyes for depth perception, a large brain relative to body size, and grasping hands — includes lemurs, monkeys, apes, and humans.

groups.name: Carnivora
groups.fact: Named for a shared ancestor's diet, not every member's — pandas and some other carnivorans eat mostly plants — but nearly all keep the order's blade-like carnassial teeth.

groups.name: Cetacea
groups.fact: Whales, dolphins and porpoises — mammals that returned to full-time ocean life, breathing air through a blowhole and giving birth to live young underwater.

groups.name: Artiodactyla
groups.fact: Even-toed hoofed mammals — cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, camels, deer and giraffes — weight-bearing carried on the third and fourth toes equally.

groups.name: Perissodactyla
groups.fact: Odd-toed hoofed mammals — horses, zebras, donkeys, and rhinoceroses — weight carried mainly on a single central toe.

groups.name: Rodentia
groups.fact: A single pair of ever-growing incisors in each jaw, worn down by constant gnawing — the largest order of mammals, over 40% of all mammal species.

groups.name: Lagomorpha
groups.fact: Rabbits, hares and pikas — often mistaken for rodents, but with an extra, tiny pair of upper incisors set behind the main pair, which rodents lack.

groups.name: Squamata
groups.fact: Lizards and snakes — the largest reptile order, unified by skin covered in overlapping horny scales and, in most, a lower jaw loosely hinged for a wide gape.

groups.name: Testudines
groups.fact: Turtles and tortoises — a bony shell fused to the spine and ribs, unique among vertebrates, with the shoulder and hip girdles inside the rib cage rather than outside it.

groups.name: Galliformes
groups.fact: Heavy-bodied, mostly ground-feeding birds — chickens, turkeys, pheasants, quail — strong legs built for scratching at the ground rather than sustained flight.

groups.name: Anseriformes
groups.fact: Waterfowl — ducks, geese and swans — webbed feet and a broad, flattened bill often edged with comb-like lamellae for filtering food from water.

groups.name: Hymenoptera
groups.fact: Bees, wasps and ants — two pairs of membranous wings linked by tiny hooks so they beat as one, and among the most social insects in the animal kingdom.

groups.name: Lepidoptera
groups.fact: Butterflies and moths — wings covered in tiny overlapping scales, which is where the order's name comes from: Greek for 'scale wing'.

groups.name: Nematoda
groups.fact: Roundworms — an unsegmented, tubular body with a fluid-filled pseudocoelom. The most numerous animal phylum by individual count; most species are free-living, but some, like Ascaris, are parasites.

groups.name: Proboscidea
groups.fact: Elephants and their extinct relatives — the only living mammal order defined by a trunk, a fusion of the nose and upper lip used for breathing, feeding, and grasping.

groups.name: Diprotodontia
groups.fact: The largest order of marsupials — kangaroos, koalas, wombats and possums — named for their two large, forward-pointing lower incisors.

groups.name: Monotremata
groups.fact: The only mammal order that lays eggs rather than giving live birth — just the platypus and four echidna species survive today.

groups.name: Lamniformes
groups.fact: Mackerel sharks — just 15 living species in 8 families, but among them the great white, the makos, the threshers, the basking shark and the goblin shark. Two of those families keep parts of their body warmer than the surrounding sea.

groups.name: Carcharhiniformes
groups.fact: Ground sharks — over 270 species, the largest shark order by far, spanning catsharks, requiem sharks and hammerheads. Nearly every member carries a nictitating membrane that draws over the eye to protect it during an attack.

groups.name: Myliobatiformes
groups.fact: Stingrays and their relatives — eagle rays, cownose rays and manta rays among them. Most carry one or more venomous barbed spines at the base of the tail; the mantas are the exception, having lost the spine entirely.

groups.name: Octopoda
groups.fact: About 300 species, all eight-armed and, since their coleoid ancestors internalised it, entirely without a shell — internal or external.

groups.name: Vampyromorphida
groups.fact: A single living species, Vampyroteuthis infernalis. Molecular studies place it as the sister group to octopuses, diverging before true squid and octopuses split.

groups.name: Oegopsida
groups.fact: Open-eyed squid — the eye has no corneal covering at all. One of several orders 'Teuthida' used to lump together before that grouping was abandoned; giant squid belongs here.

groups.name: Nautilida
groups.fact: A once-diverse order reduced to a single family today, Nautilidae — the only living cephalopods that still carry an external shell.

groups.name: Anthozoa
groups.fact: Corals, sea anemones and their relatives — every one of them spends its whole life as a polyp. No cnidarian in this group ever has a free-swimming medusa stage.

groups.name: Hexacorallia
groups.fact: Anthozoans built on six-fold symmetry — stony reef-building corals and sea anemones both belong here, against the eight-fold symmetry of the soft corals in Octocorallia.

groups.name: Actiniaria
groups.fact: True sea anemones — solitary polyps with no skeleton at all, holding their shape with a hydrostatic skeleton of fluid instead.

groups.name: Medusozoa
groups.fact: Cnidarians whose life cycle includes a free-swimming medusa stage — the bell-and-tentacles body plan most people picture when they hear 'jellyfish'.

groups.name: Scyphozoa
groups.fact: The 'true' jellyfish. A single sessile polyp buds off a stack of young medusae, one at a time, in a process called strobilation.

groups.name: Cubozoa
groups.fact: Box jellyfish were classed as an order of Scyphozoa until 1973, when their own life cycle and their true, lensed eyes earned them a class of their own.

groups.name: Hydrozoa
groups.fact: The most varied cnidarian class — solitary hydroids and colonial siphonophores both belong here, most alternating between a polyp stage and a medusa stage.

groups.name: Siphonophorae
groups.fact: Colonies built from specialised zooids that bud from one fertilised egg and stay fused — no single member could survive alone, but the colony functions as one animal.

groups.name: Asteroidea
groups.fact: Starfish — about 1,900 species, moving on a hydraulic water-vascular system of fluid-filled canals, and many able to regrow an entire lost arm.

groups.name: Orectolobiformes
groups.fact: Carpet sharks — around 43 species in 7 families, with a small mouth that never extends past the eyes and, in most species, a pair of sensory barbels beside the nostrils. Bottom-dwelling nurse and wobbegong sharks belong here, and so does the whale shark, the largest fish alive.

groups.name: Lophiiformes
groups.fact: Anglerfishes — about 13 families united by the illicium, a modified fin ray tipped with a lure called the esca that draws prey close. In deep-sea species the esca glows, lit by colonies of symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria.

groups.name: Perciformes
groups.fact: Once defined so broadly it held around 41% of all bony fish species, until molecular studies split most of that apart. What's left has since absorbed the former orders Scorpaeniformes and Gasterosteiformes, so groupers, lionfish and stonefish now classify here too, alongside perches and basses.

groups.name: Felidae
groups.fact: Retractile claws and carnassial teeth built for tearing and cutting flesh — every one of the 41 living species is an obligate carnivore, meat is not optional.

groups.name: Pantherinae
groups.fact: The 'big cat' subfamily — five Panthera species plus the two clouded leopards — split from the rest of Felidae in the Miocene, roughly 6 to 10 million years ago.

groups.name: Machairodontinae
groups.fact: The sabertooth cats — elongated upper canines, the earliest-diverging branch of the whole cat family, and gone since the end-Pleistocene extinction with no living descendants.

groups.name: Panthera
groups.fact: Tiger, lion, jaguar, leopard and snow leopard — unified by an incompletely ossified hyoid bone and an elastic-padded larynx that lets every member roar, except the snow leopard.

groups.name: Canidae
groups.fact: Long legs and a lithe body built for chasing prey, non-retractable claws, and carnassial teeth shaped for shearing flesh — around 37 living species, from the 24 cm fennec fox to the gray wolf.

groups.name: Canis
groups.fact: Wolves, coyotes, jackals and the domestic dog — every species here has 78 chromosomes and can potentially interbreed with every other.

groups.name: Canis lupus
groups.fact: One species holding the gray wolf and every domestic dog breed alike — Canis lupus familiaris is formally a subspecies of the wolf, not a separate species, and the dingo is another.

groups.name: Gadiformes
groups.fact: Cod, hake, haddock and their relatives — nearly all marine, mostly cold-water, with pelvic fins set below or ahead of the pectorals. Many are major commercial food fish; the burbot is the order's only fully freshwater member.

groups.name: Clupeiformes
groups.fact: Herring, sardines, anchovies and shad — silvery, spindle-shaped schooling fish that make up many of the ocean's most important forage species, feeding an enormous share of everything above them in the food web.

groups.name: Salmoniformes
groups.fact: Salmon and trout in one suborder, pike and mudminnows in the other — two lineages closely enough related to sit in a single order, united by a small rayless adipose fin between the dorsal fin and the tail.

groups.name: Cypriniformes
groups.fact: Carp, goldfish, koi, minnows and loaches — over 4,200 species with no teeth in the jaw at all; instead they grind food with pharyngeal teeth in the throat, working against a pad at the base of the skull.

groups.name: Anguilliformes
groups.fact: True eels — about 1,000 species with no pelvic fins, dorsal and anal fins fused into a single ribbon running most of the body's length, and a flat, transparent larval stage called a leptocephalus found in no other fish order.

groups.name: Siluriformes
groups.fact: Catfish — roughly one in twenty of all vertebrate species alive, none of them scaled, most named for the whisker-like barbels around the mouth that smell and feel for food in murky water.

groups.name: Carangiformes
groups.fact: Once just the jacks and trevallies, this order has absorbed a wide swath of the old Perciformes as genetic studies reorganised the bony-fish tree — jacks, barracudas, remoras, flatfishes, swordfish and marlin now all classify here together.

groups.name: Syngnathiformes
groups.fact: Seahorses, pipefish and their relatives — a tubular, toothless snout that sucks in prey at close range, and in most species the male, not the female, carries the fertilised eggs to term.

groups.name: Blenniiformes
groups.fact: Blennies and damselfish — including the anemonefish — sat scattered across the old order Perciformes until genetic studies showed they form their own lineage; Eschmeyer's Catalog of Fishes now groups them here instead.

groups.name: Characiformes
groups.fact: Piranhas and tetras share this order's defining feature, a Weberian apparatus — a chain of small bones linking the swim bladder to the inner ear, sharpening hearing in fresh water.

groups.name: Centrarchiformes
groups.fact: North American sunfish and bass on one branch, Australian grunters and hawkfishes on another — recently split out of Perciformes, and still missing from some textbooks even as fish databases now accept it.

groups.name: Coleoptera
groups.fact: Beetles — the largest insect order by far, with more described species than any other order in the animal kingdom. Defined by a hardened pair of forewings, elytra, that meet in a straight line down the back and cover the flight wings beneath.

groups.name: Odonata
groups.fact: Dragonflies and damselflies — one of the oldest still-living insect lineages, with a fossil record going back over 300 million years, long before dinosaurs.

groups.name: Orthoptera
groups.fact: Grasshoppers, crickets and locusts — powerful hind legs built for jumping, and in most species, sound produced by rubbing one body part against another.

groups.name: Mantodea
groups.fact: Praying mantises — an elongated thorax and a pair of spiked, grasping forelegs held folded in front of the body, ready to snap out at passing prey.

groups.name: Blattodea
groups.fact: Cockroaches, and, nested inside them as their closest living relatives, termites — a group united by molecular evidence more than by looks.

groups.name: Siphonaptera
groups.fact: Fleas — wingless, laterally flattened, and built almost entirely around one skill: jumping onto a passing host to feed on its blood.

groups.name: Araneae
groups.fact: Spiders — every one of the roughly 50,000 described species has silk-producing spinnerets and fanged chelicerae, though not every species spins a web to catch prey.

groups.name: Scorpiones
groups.fact: Scorpions — a pair of grasping pedipalps and a narrow, segmented tail ending in a venomous stinger, the telson. Unusually among arachnids, every species gives birth to live young.

groups.name: Ixodida
groups.fact: Ticks — obligate blood-feeders at every stage past the egg, and the primary route by which diseases like Lyme disease pass from wildlife into people.

groups.name: Chilopoda
groups.fact: Centipedes — fast, venomous predators with exactly one pair of legs per body segment, injected through forcipules, a modified front pair of legs rather than fangs.

groups.name: Diplopoda
groups.fact: Millipedes — slow-moving detritivores with two pairs of legs per body segment, twice a centipede's count, and no species with anywhere near 1,000 legs.

groups.name: Isopoda
groups.fact: Isopods — seven pairs of walking legs and a body of overlapping plates. Most are marine, but the woodlice of suborder Oniscidea are the only crustaceans to have fully adapted to life on dry land.

groups.name: Dinosauria
groups.fact: Defined by hip and hindlimb traits that hold the body upright, off to the side, rather than sprawled like a lizard's — includes every dinosaur that ever lived, and, since birds are its one surviving lineage, still does.

groups.name: Saurischia
groups.fact: The 'lizard-hipped' dinosaurs, named for a pubis bone pointed forward as in a lizard — an ironic name, since this is the saurischian line, not the 'bird-hipped' Ornithischia, that actually gave rise to birds.

groups.name: Ornithischia
groups.fact: The 'bird-hipped' dinosaurs, named for a backward-pointed pubis bone that happens to resemble a bird's — despite the name, every living bird actually descends from the other dinosaur lineage, Saurischia.

groups.name: Theropoda
groups.fact: Bipedal, mostly meat-eating dinosaurs, hollow-boned and three-toed — and the only dinosaur lineage with living members, since every bird alive today is technically a theropod.

groups.name: Sauropodomorpha
groups.fact: Long-necked, small-headed herbivorous dinosaurs, running from early bipedal forms through the four-legged giants of Sauropoda — the largest land animals that have ever lived.

groups.name: Thyreophora
groups.fact: Armoured herbivorous dinosaurs, defined as everything closer to Ankylosaurus and Stegosaurus than to Iguanodon or Triceratops — rows of bony plates or spikes set into the skin distinguish the group across 130 million years.

groups.name: Marginocephalia
groups.fact: Herbivorous dinosaurs sharing a bony shelf or margin at the back of the skull — in ceratopsians it flares into a frill, in pachycephalosaurs it thickens into a dome.

groups.name: Ornithopoda
groups.fact: Beaked, mostly bipedal-capable herbivorous dinosaurs with increasingly sophisticated batteries of grinding teeth — the line that runs from small early browsers up to the duck-billed hadrosaurs.

groups.name: Coelurosauria
groups.fact: Every theropod closer to birds than to Allosaurus — tyrannosaurs, ostrich-mimics, raptors and birds all belong here, and fossil skin impressions show even its earliest members were feathered.

groups.name: Megalosauroidea
groups.fact: A lineage of large-bodied theropods including the spinosaurids — sail- or ridge-backed, often long-snouted predators adapted, in several members, to hunting near or in water.

groups.name: Carnosauria
groups.fact: Large predatory theropods closer to Allosaurus than to living birds — a group that, despite the name's old association with the biggest meat-eaters, does not include Tyrannosaurus, which classifies elsewhere, in Coelurosauria.

groups.name: Paraves
groups.fact: Every theropod closer to living birds than to the oviraptorosaurs — split between the sickle-clawed Deinonychosauria and Avialae, the birds themselves. It is the clade where the line between 'dinosaur' and 'bird' gets genuinely hard to draw.

groups.name: Deinonychosauria
groups.fact: The 'raptors' — dromaeosaurids and troodontids — small to mid-sized feathered theropods best known for an enlarged, sickle-shaped claw on the second toe of each foot.

groups.name: Sauropoda
groups.fact: Four-legged, long-necked, long-tailed herbivores with small heads and pillar-like legs — the largest land animals ever to exist, some reaching well over 30 metres long.

groups.name: Stegosauria
groups.fact: Thyreophorans carrying rows of upright plates or spikes down the back and tail rather than the fused armour of their ankylosaur relatives.

groups.name: Ankylosauria
groups.fact: Heavily armoured, low-slung thyreophorans covered in fused bony plates called osteoderms, several with a stiffened, weaponised tail tip.

groups.name: Ceratopsia
groups.fact: Beaked, herbivorous dinosaurs running from small, largely bipedal early forms to the massive horned, frilled quadrupeds of the Late Cretaceous.

groups.name: Pachycephalosauria
groups.fact: Thick-skulled, mostly bipedal herbivores whose skull roof thickened, in some species, into a solid dome believed to have been used in head-to-head combat.

groups.name: Iguanodontia
groups.fact: Beaked ornithopods running from Iguanodon-grade forms up through the duck-billed hadrosaurs nested inside it — what were once called separate 'iguanodontid' families are now understood as steps along one continuous lineage.

groups.name: Tyrannosauridae
groups.fact: Large-bodied coelurosaurs with deep, massive skulls, tiny two-fingered forelimbs and bone-crushing bite force — Tyrannosaurus is the largest and last-surviving member.

groups.name: Compsognathidae
groups.fact: Small, lightly built coelurosaurs, among them some of the smallest dinosaurs known — Compsognathus itself once held that record.

groups.name: Brachiosauridae
groups.fact: Sauropods with forelimbs longer than their hindlimbs, tilting the body into a steep, giraffe-like incline built for browsing well above the heads of other sauropods.

groups.name: Diplodocidae
groups.fact: Extremely long, whip-tailed sauropods with comparatively slender builds and squared, peg-toothed snouts suited to stripping low vegetation — Apatosaurus and Diplodocus both belong here.

groups.name: Protoceratopsidae
groups.fact: Small, mostly hornless early ceratopsians with a bony frill already present but not yet the huge horns of their later ceratopsid cousins — a real side-branch of the family, not a direct ancestor of them.

groups.name: Ceratopsidae
groups.fact: The large, quadrupedal, horned ceratopsians of the Late Cretaceous — Triceratops among them — carrying the group's biggest horns and most elaborate frills.

groups.name: Hadrosauridae
groups.fact: The 'duck-billed dinosaurs' — the most derived branch of Iguanodontia, with broad, toothless beaks backed by hundreds of grinding teeth, and in several lineages, elaborate hollow head crests.

groups.name: Pterosauria
groups.fact: Flying reptiles that shared the Mesozoic skies with the dinosaurs below them — close archosaur relatives of Dinosauria, but not dinosaurs themselves; wings formed from a skin membrane stretched to a hugely elongated fourth finger.

groups.name: Azhdarchidae
groups.fact: Large to enormous late Cretaceous pterosaurs with long, stiffened necks and long jaws — the group that includes Quetzalcoatlus, a leading contender for the largest flying animal ever known.

groups.name: Plesiosauria
groups.fact: Marine reptiles with four flipper-like limbs, found from the Early Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous — swimming alongside the dinosaurs, in the same seas, but no closer to them than any other reptile group.

groups.name: Elasmosauridae
groups.fact: Plesiosaurs with the most extreme necks in the group, built from as many as 70 or more vertebrae — Elasmosaurus itself carried 72, among the highest counts known.

groups.name: Leptocyon
groups.fact: The earliest known lineage within Caninae, small fox-like omnivores that persisted almost unchanged through the Oligocene and Miocene of North America.

groups.name: Eucyon
groups.fact: A jackal-sized Miocene canid, and the genus most directly responsible for spreading the canine lineage out of North America and into Eurasia.

groups.name: Plantae
groups.fact: Multicellular eukaryotes that make their own food by photosynthesis, walled in cellulose rather than the chitin of a fungus or the flexible membrane of an animal cell.

groups.name: Bryophyta
groups.fact: Mosses: no roots, just thread-like rhizoids for grip, and no xylem or phloem to move water internally — every cell is close enough to the surface to hydrate on its own.

groups.name: Marchantiophyta
groups.fact: Liverworts: among the very first plant lineages to leave the water, over 470 million years ago, still dependent like mosses on a film of surface water for their sperm to swim through.

groups.name: Tracheophyta
groups.fact: Vascular plants: internal piping — xylem for water, phloem for sugar — that lets a plant stand tall and move resources far from where roots or leaves actually are.

groups.name: Polypodiopsida
groups.fact: Ferns: vascular, but reproducing by spore rather than seed or flower, with fronds that typically unfurl from a tight coil called a fiddlehead.

groups.name: Polypodiales
groups.fact: The largest order of ferns by far, holding roughly 80% of all living fern species — nearly every fern you're likely to recognise sits somewhere inside it.

groups.name: Dennstaedtiaceae
groups.fact: A family of mostly coarse, fast-spreading ferns, several of them — bracken among them — able to dominate open, disturbed ground more aggressively than almost any other fern.

groups.name: Pteridium
groups.fact: Bracken — a genus of just a handful of species, but between them one of the most widely distributed plant genera on Earth, native to every continent except Antarctica.

groups.name: Spermatophyta
groups.fact: Seed plants: an embryo packaged with its own food supply inside a protective coat, able to lie dormant for years rather than needing water on hand the moment it's released.

groups.name: Pinophyta
groups.fact: Conifers: cone-bearing, mostly evergreen, needle- or scale-leaved gymnosperms — seed plants that never evolved a flower or a fruit around the seed.

groups.name: Cupressales
groups.fact: Cypresses and their relatives — one of the two great living conifer orders, and the one that holds the redwoods and giant sequoia alongside junipers and true cypresses.

groups.name: Cupressaceae
groups.fact: The cypress family — around 30 genera worldwide, spanning scale-leaved hedge cypresses, junipers, and the three redwood genera of subfamily Sequoioideae.

groups.name: Sequoioideae
groups.fact: The redwood subfamily: just three living genera left of a once wider group — Sequoia on the California coast, Sequoiadendron in the Sierra Nevada, and Metasequoia in China.

groups.name: Sequoiadendron
groups.fact: A monotypic genus — one living species, the giant sequoia — with a fossil record reaching back to the Late Cretaceous, over 66 million years before the present.

groups.name: Sequoia
groups.fact: Also monotypic today, holding only the coast redwood — sister genus to Sequoiadendron, though the two split onto opposite sides of California long ago.

groups.name: Gnetophyta
groups.fact: The strangest gymnosperms: just three surviving genera — Gnetum, Ephedra and Welwitschia — sharing vessel elements in their wood, a feature otherwise almost exclusive to flowering plants.

groups.name: Welwitschiales
groups.fact: An order containing a single family and a single genus — Welwitschia — one of the most extreme cases of taxonomic isolation among living plants.

groups.name: Welwitschiaceae
groups.fact: A monotypic family built around one desert-adapted genus, Welwitschia, found nowhere but a narrow strip of the Namib Desert coast.

groups.name: Welwitschia
groups.fact: One living species, Welwitschia mirabilis, growing just two strap-shaped leaves for its entire lifetime — some individuals estimated at close to 2,000 years old.

groups.name: Angiospermae
groups.fact: Flowering plants: seeds enclosed inside an ovary that ripens into fruit — over 300,000 species, by far the largest and most diverse group of living plants.

groups.name: Nymphaeales
groups.fact: Water lilies and their relatives sit among the earliest-diverging lineages of flowering plants — branching off near the base of the angiosperm family tree, close behind Amborella.

groups.name: Nymphaeaceae
groups.fact: The true water lily family — floating or emergent aquatic herbs rooted in mud, with air-channelled leaves and stems built to keep submerged tissue oxygenated.

groups.name: Nymphaea
groups.fact: The true water lilies, and the genus that gives the whole family its name — around 50 species found on every continent except Antarctica.

groups.name: Monocots
groups.fact: Flowering plants with a single seed leaf, parallel-veined leaves, and vascular bundles scattered through the stem rather than arranged in a ring — grasses, palms and orchids among them.

groups.name: Alismatales
groups.fact: A monocot order unusually rich in aquatic and wetland plants — pondweeds, arrowheads, seagrasses and the arum family all sit inside it.

groups.name: Araceae
groups.fact: The arum family — from towering titan arums down to duckweed, now classified inside this family as subfamily Lemnoideae despite once being ranked as its own family entirely.

groups.name: Lemnoideae
groups.fact: Duckweeds: flowering plants reduced to a floating frond a few millimetres across at most, with the genus Wolffia holding the smallest flower of any plant known, just 0.3mm long.

groups.name: Asparagales
groups.fact: A large monocot order — asparagus, agaves, irises and, most diverse of all its families, the orchids.

groups.name: Orchidaceae
groups.fact: One of the two largest families of flowering plants, around 28,000 species, most producing seeds so fine and food-free that they need a mycorrhizal fungus just to germinate.

groups.name: Eudicots
groups.fact: The larger of the two great flowering-plant lineages — pollen with three furrows rather than one, and typically two seed leaves rather than a monocot's single one.

groups.name: Caryophyllales
groups.fact: An order that unites cacti, beets and carnations with two entire carnivorous-plant families — Droseraceae and Nepenthaceae both evolved their traps somewhere inside it.

groups.name: Droseraceae
groups.fact: Three genera — Drosera, Dionaea and Aldrovanda — sharing one carnivorous ancestor; molecular evidence shows the two snap-trap genera are each other's closest relative, so the snap trap evolved only once.

groups.name: Dionaea
groups.fact: A single living species, the Venus flytrap, native to nowhere but a small patch of the Carolinas — one of the most geographically restricted carnivorous plants on Earth.

groups.name: Drosera
groups.fact: The sundews — at least 194 species, making this the largest genus of carnivorous plants by far, unified by sticky, glistening, dew-like traps on every leaf.

groups.name: Nepenthaceae
groups.fact: A monotypic family holding only the genus Nepenthes, the tropical pitcher plants, concentrated on Borneo, Sumatra and the Philippines.

groups.name: Nepenthes
groups.fact: The tropical pitcher plants, trapping prey passively — no moving parts, just a slippery wax-lined pitfall baited with nectar around the rim.

groups.name: Cactaceae
groups.fact: The cactus family, almost entirely native to the Americas — around 1,750 species, nearly all running photosynthesis backwards, opening their pores at night rather than by day.

groups.name: Carnegiea
groups.fact: A single living species, the saguaro — the columnar giant of the Sonoran Desert, named for the steel magnate Andrew Carnegie.

groups.name: Santalales
groups.fact: An order unusually full of parasites — sandalwoods and mistletoes both belong here, tapping into a host plant's tissue rather than making everything they need from scratch.

groups.name: Santalaceae
groups.fact: The sandalwood family, expanded in modern classification to absorb the former mistletoe family Viscaceae — Viscum, the type genus of true mistletoe, sits inside it.

groups.name: Viscum
groups.fact: True mistletoe — around 100 hemiparasitic species, each tapping a host tree's xylem through a haustorium while still photosynthesising with its own green leaves.

groups.name: Malpighiales
groups.fact: A huge, famously hard-to-define eudicot order — willows and violets sit here alongside Rafflesiaceae, whose giant flowers gave no visual hint of the relationship until DNA evidence forced the reclassification.

groups.name: Rafflesiaceae
groups.fact: Just three genera and around 36 species, every one a leafless, stemless, rootless parasite living inside a host vine until it's time to flower.

groups.name: Rafflesia
groups.fact: The genus that includes Rafflesia arnoldii, whose flower — at over a metre across and up to 10kg — is the largest single bloom of any flowering plant on Earth.

groups.name: Asterales
groups.fact: An order dominated by one family, Asteraceae, whose flower heads pack dozens or hundreds of tiny individual flowers into what looks, from a bee's-eye view, like a single bloom.

groups.name: Asteraceae
groups.fact: The daisy family — one of the two largest families of flowering plants, its 'flower' almost always a composite head of many small florets crowded together.

groups.name: Leontopodium
groups.fact: The edelweiss genus — around 30-40 species of small, woolly-haired alpine daisies across the mountains of Europe and Asia.

groups.name: Fungi
groups.fact: Eukaryotes with cell walls of chitin rather than cellulose, feeding by secreting enzymes onto their food and absorbing the result — neither eating it like an animal nor making it by photosynthesis like a plant.

groups.name: Basidiomycota
groups.fact: Reproduces sexually via club-shaped cells called basidia, each usually bearing spores externally — about 31,500 species, including most mushrooms, puffballs, bracket fungi, rusts and smuts.

groups.name: Ascomycota
groups.fact: The largest fungal phylum, over 64,000 species, defined by the ascus — a microscopic sac in which spores form internally, unlike the external spores of Basidiomycota.

groups.name: Agaricales
groups.fact: Around 46 families, 400-plus genera and over 25,000 described species — the classic gilled mushrooms, but also non-agaric forms like puffballs and coral fungi that molecular studies placed here.

groups.name: Cantharellales
groups.fact: United less by looks than by microscopic structure — spindle-shaped nuclei arranged lengthwise in the basidia — a group spanning chanterelles, tooth fungi and coral-like clavarioid fungi.

groups.name: Boletales
groups.fact: Over 1,300 species with a surprising range of fruiting-body shapes, uniting the pored boletes with agarics, puffballs and other forms that turn out to be close relatives underneath.

groups.name: Phallales
groups.fact: Around 195 species across three families, best known for the stinkhorns — fruiting bodies that skip wind dispersal entirely and instead smell of carrion to recruit flies as spore carriers.

groups.name: Polyporales
groups.fact: About 1,800 species of wood-decaying fungi, breaking timber down either by white rot, which strips out lignin, or brown rot, which strips out cellulose instead.

groups.name: Tremellales
groups.fact: Gelatinous fruiting bodies, and nearly every species that produces one is a parasite of another fungus rather than an independent decomposer — the yeast phase of the life cycle is the free-living exception.

groups.name: Pezizales
groups.fact: About 1,683 species whose asci pop open through a hinged lid, an operculum — a group spanning morels, truffles and ordinary cup fungi across soil, wood and dung.

groups.name: Hypocreales
groups.fact: Identified in the field by vividly coloured spore-producing structures — yellow, orange or red — and containing many of the fungi that parasitise insects, other fungi or plants rather than decomposing dead matter.

groups.name: Xylariales
groups.fact: About 164 genera across 22 families, built around dense, often charcoal-black fungal tissue called a stroma — living as endophytes inside plants, as pathogens, or as decomposers of wood.

groups.name: Amanitaceae
groups.fact: Mushrooms that emerge from an egg-like universal veil, mostly in the genus Amanita — a family holding both prized edibles and the species responsible for over half of all fatal mushroom poisonings.

groups.name: Mycenaceae
groups.fact: Small saprobic mushrooms of worldwide distribution, split out of the old family Tricholomataceae once DNA sequencing showed genera like Mycena and Panellus formed their own separate branch.

groups.name: Agaricaceae
groups.fact: About 85 genera and 1,340 species, headed by the commercially important genus Agaricus and now also holding groups once classified separately, among them several ink caps and parasol mushrooms.

groups.name: Physalacriaceae
groups.fact: A family running from arctic to tropical habitat and even into fresh water, holding the genus Armillaria — among them the organism argued to be the largest living thing on Earth.

groups.name: Nidulariaceae
groups.fact: The bird's nest fungi — five genera whose fruiting bodies form tiny cup-shaped 'nests' holding egg-like peridioles, built specifically to be launched out by a falling raindrop.

groups.name: Cantharellaceae
groups.fact: The chanterelles and their relatives, with a smooth, wrinkled or blunt-ridged spore-bearing surface rather than the sharp true gills of an ordinary mushroom.

groups.name: Boletaceae
groups.fact: About 59 genera of mushrooms with small pores instead of gills on the underside of the cap, most forming ectomycorrhizal partnerships with the roots of trees and shrubs.

groups.name: Phallaceae
groups.fact: The stinkhorn family proper — around 21 genera and 77 species whose foul-smelling spore slime draws flies, beetles and other insects in to carry the spores away.

groups.name: Polyporaceae
groups.fact: About 114 genera and 1,621 species of wood-decaying fungi carrying their fertile layer in vertical pores on the underside of the cap, the origin of the common name 'polypore'.

groups.name: Tremellaceae
groups.fact: Now narrowed to a single genus, Tremella, with around 40 species of gelatinous fungi whose sexual form is almost always a parasite living on the mycelium of a different fungus.

groups.name: Morchellaceae
groups.fact: Fruiting bodies that are pitted and sponge-like in Morchella, thimble-shaped in Verpa, or shallow and cup-like in Disciotis, alongside several lesser-known genera that fruit entirely underground.

groups.name: Tuberaceae
groups.fact: A family of mycorrhizal fungi that evolved during the Jurassic, holding the genus Tuber — true truffles — alongside several rarer genera of underground fungi.

groups.name: Ophiocordycipitaceae
groups.fact: A family of parasitic fungi holding Ophiocordyceps and several related genera, many of which infect and kill insects and other arthropods as their normal way of life.

groups.name: Xylariaceae
groups.fact: Mostly small, dark-fruited fungi that decay wood and colonise other dead plant material, found across both temperate and tropical regions worldwide.

groups.name: Amanita
groups.fact: About 600 described species, identifiable by a ring and a cup-like volva on the stem, free gills and a white spore print — and responsible for around 95% of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide.

groups.name: Felinae
groups.fact: Every Felidae species except Panthera and the two clouded leopards — 32 species from the domestic cat to the cheetah and cougar, none of them able to roar.

groups.name: Felis
groups.fact: Seven small-cat species, from the domestic cat to the black-footed and jungle cats — pupils that contract to a vertical slit, not a circle.

groups.name: Acinonyx
groups.fact: A single living species, the cheetah — claws that stay only semi-retracted, unlike almost every other cat, for extra grip during its high-speed chase.

groups.name: Puma
groups.fact: Two living species, the cougar and the small, tropical jaguarundi — the cougar alone has the widest range of any wild land mammal in the Americas.

groups.name: Vulpes
groups.fact: Twelve living species of true fox — the red fox among them by far the most abundant and widely distributed of the group.

groups.name: Lycaon
groups.fact: A single living species, the African wild dog — big rounded ears, and only four toes per foot, one fewer than every other canid.

groups.name: Canis latrans
groups.fact: The coyote — able to interbreed with wolves and domestic dogs alike, since every species in genus Canis shares the same 78 chromosomes.

groups.name: Ursidae
groups.fact: Eight living bear species share plantigrade feet and non-retractable claws, and nearly all are broadly omnivorous despite sitting inside the meat-eating order Carnivora.

groups.name: Ursus
groups.fact: Six of the eight living bear species, including the brown and polar bears — the polar bear is the most carnivorous of the family, and the largest living land carnivore.

groups.name: Ailuropoda
groups.fact: A single living species, the giant panda — the only bear whose diet is almost entirely bamboo.

groups.name: Helarctos
groups.fact: A single living species, the sun bear — the smallest of all eight bears, built for climbing trees and prying open rotten logs.

groups.name: Hominidae
groups.fact: The great apes — gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans and humans, sharing a common ancestor, and every genus but the orangutan getting around on the ground by knuckle-walking.

groups.name: Gorilla
groups.fact: Two living gorilla species, split from each other roughly two million years ago by the Congo river basin lying between them.

groups.name: Pan
groups.fact: Humans' closest living relatives — the chimpanzee and the bonobo — sharing roughly 98% of their DNA with us.

groups.name: Pongo
groups.fact: Three orangutan species, all critically endangered and all confined to the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra.

groups.name: Cercopithecidae
groups.fact: The Old World monkeys — over 130 species, set apart from apes by a tail and from New World monkeys by narrow, downward-pointing nostrils.

groups.name: Papio
groups.fact: Six baboon species, among the largest monkeys alive and, unusually for a primate, mostly ground-dwelling rather than arboreal.

groups.name: Lemuridae
groups.fact: A family found nowhere on Earth outside Madagascar and the small islands around it.

groups.name: Lemur
groups.fact: A single living species, the ring-tailed lemur — the most terrestrial of all lemurs, spending far more of its day on the ground than its tree-bound relatives.

groups.name: Accipitriformes
groups.fact: Diurnal birds of prey with strongly hooked bills and powerful grasping talons — eagles, hawks and kites among them.

groups.name: Accipitridae
groups.fact: The largest family of daytime raptors, hunting mainly by keen eyesight rather than the scent- or hearing-led methods some other predators rely on.

groups.name: Haliaeetus
groups.fact: The sea eagles — eight species built around fishing, with bare, unfeathered legs and a strong preference for hunting near open water.

groups.name: Falconiformes
groups.fact: Falcons and their relatives — a lineage genetics places closer to parrots and songbirds than to the hawks and eagles they superficially resemble.

groups.name: Falconidae
groups.fact: Falcons kill with a notched, tooth-like edge on the beak that severs a prey animal's spinal cord, rather than crushing it with the feet the way a hawk or eagle does.

groups.name: Falco
groups.fact: About 40 species of true falcon, from the sparrow-sized kestrels to the peregrine — the fastest animal on Earth in its hunting dive.

groups.name: Strigiformes
groups.fact: Owls — roughly 250 species of mostly nocturnal raptor, with forward-facing eyes fixed in their sockets and a head that swivels to compensate.

groups.name: Strigidae
groups.fact: The 'true owls,' set apart from barn owls by a round rather than heart-shaped facial disc.

groups.name: Bubo
groups.fact: The largest living owls sit in this genus, the snowy owl and the eagle-owls among them.

groups.name: Cathartiformes
groups.fact: New World vultures — sometimes classed as their own order, sometimes folded into Accipitriformes, but genuinely unrelated to Old World vultures despite the resemblance.

groups.name: Cathartidae
groups.fact: Seven living species, unified less by shared ancestry with other raptors than by having independently evolved the same scavenging lifestyle as Old World vultures.

groups.name: Cathartes
groups.fact: Three vulture species, the turkey vulture among them — one of the very few birds with a genuinely useful sense of smell.

groups.name: Anura
groups.fact: Frogs and toads — over 7,000 species, unified by a tailless adult body built around powerful hind legs for jumping.

groups.name: Dendrobatidae
groups.fact: The poison dart frogs — small, brightly coloured, and many genuinely toxic in the wild, though captive-bred individuals typically lose the toxin entirely.

groups.name: Phyllobates
groups.fact: Just five species, but the most toxic of all the dart frogs — Phyllobates terribilis alone carries enough poison to kill several grown adults.

groups.name: Ranidae
groups.fact: The 'true frogs' — a huge, nearly worldwide family of smooth-skinned, long-legged frogs, most of them strong jumpers and swimmers.

groups.name: Lithobates
groups.fact: North American true frogs, the American bullfrog among them — some taxonomists still fold this genus back into the older, broader Rana.

groups.name: Bufonidae
groups.fact: The 'true toads' — squat, warty-skinned frogs, nearly all of them carrying toxin-secreting parotoid glands behind the eyes.

groups.name: Rhinella
groups.fact: South and Central American toads, the cane toad among them — introduced far outside this genus's native range as a would-be pest-control agent, with disastrous results.

groups.name: Caudata
groups.fact: Salamanders and newts — the only living amphibians that keep a tail into adulthood, and the group with the greatest capacity of any vertebrate for regenerating lost limbs.

groups.name: Ambystomatidae
groups.fact: The mole salamanders, named for spending most of their lives burrowed underground — except for a handful of species, the axolotl among them, that never leave the water at all.

groups.name: Ambystoma
groups.fact: About 32 species of mole salamander, native only to North America.

groups.name: Salamandridae
groups.fact: The 'true salamanders' and newts — a family whose members are, almost without exception, defended by toxic skin secretions.

groups.name: Salamandra
groups.fact: The genus that gives salamanders their name — Salamandra salamandra, the fire salamander, is its best-known member.

groups.name: Elapidae
groups.fact: Front-fanged venomous snakes with short, permanently erect fangs — cobras, mambas, coral snakes and sea snakes all belong here.

groups.name: Ophiophagus
groups.fact: The king cobra — the longest venomous snake alive, and closer kin to the mambas than to the true cobras, despite the common name.

groups.name: Varanidae
groups.fact: The monitor lizards — every living species falls into a single genus, Varanus, found across Africa, Asia and Australia.

groups.name: Varanus
groups.fact: About 80 monitor lizard species, spanning from lizards smaller than a house cat to the three-metre Komodo dragon.

groups.name: Helodermatidae
groups.fact: Just two living species worldwide — the Gila monster and the Mexican beaded lizard — the only venomous lizards outside the monitor lineage.

groups.name: Heloderma
groups.fact: Delivers venom by chewing it into a wound through grooved teeth, rather than injecting it through hollow fangs the way a snake does.

groups.name: Crocodylia
groups.fact: Crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials — the closest living relatives birds have among the reptiles, the last two survivors of the Archosauria.

groups.name: Crocodylidae
groups.fact: True crocodiles — their lower fourth tooth fits into a groove on the outside of the upper jaw and stays visible even with the mouth closed.

groups.name: Crocodylus
groups.fact: About 13 living crocodile species, the Nile crocodile among them — one of the most dangerous large predators to humans anywhere in the world.

groups.name: Alligatoridae
groups.fact: Alligators and caimans — a broader, more U-shaped snout than a crocodile's, and lower teeth that fit into sockets on the inside of the upper jaw, hidden when the mouth is shut.

groups.name: Alligator
groups.fact: Just two living species — the American alligator and the far rarer Chinese alligator, the only other member of the genus.

groups.name: Herrerasauria
groups.fact: An early saurischian lineage among the very earliest known dinosaurs, so close to the theropod/sauropodomorph split its own branch is still debated.

groups.name: Ceratosauria
groups.fact: Theropods sharing a more recent common ancestor with Ceratosaurus than with birds — mostly Southern Hemisphere predators with ornamented skulls and short forelimbs.

groups.name: Abelisauridae
groups.fact: Stocky-legged ceratosaurian predators of Cretaceous Gondwana, with ornate, pitted skulls and forelimbs reduced almost to uselessness.

groups.name: Carcharodontosauridae
groups.fact: Carnosaurs that rivaled Tyrannosaurus for largest land predator ever, with blade-like serrated teeth built for slicing rather than crushing bone.

groups.name: Spinosauridae
groups.fact: Long-snouted, crocodile-skulled megalosauroids with conical teeth, some carrying tall sail-like neural spines, adapted toward hunting fish.

groups.name: Therizinosauria
groups.fact: Herbivorous coelurosaurs with the longest claws of any known animal, a long neck, and hips that convergently resemble an ornithischian's.

groups.name: Oviraptorosauria
groups.fact: Feathered, beaked, mostly toothless maniraptorans, some crested like a cassowary — among the theropods closest to birds.

groups.name: Ornithomimosauria
groups.fact: Ostrich-mimic coelurosaurs — long-legged, small-headed and fast, ranging in diet from omnivorous to herbivorous.

groups.name: Psittacosauridae
groups.fact: The earliest well-known ceratopsians, an early offshoot rather than a direct ancestor of the later horned, frilled forms.

groups.name: Centrosaurinae
groups.fact: Ceratopsids with a large nose horn, short brow horns and elaborately spiked frills, known mostly from western North America.

groups.name: Chasmosaurinae
groups.fact: Ceratopsids with long, prominent brow horns and long frills carrying little spiking, unlike Centrosaurinae's shorter-horned, heavier ornamentation.

groups.name: Rhinocerotidae
groups.fact: Five living rhinoceros species on massive, thick-skinned bodies -- the two African species carry two horns, the three Asian species one horn or none.

groups.name: Rhinoceros
groups.fact: Two living species, the Indian and Javan rhinoceros, each carrying a single horn and skin thrown into deep folds that give it an armor-plated look.

groups.name: Hyaenidae
groups.fact: Just four living species, and despite a dog-like build, genetically closer to cats and mongooses than to any canid -- hyenas sit in the cat-like suborder Feliformes, not the dog-like Caniformes.

groups.name: Crocuta
groups.fact: A single living species, the spotted hyena -- the largest hyena, and unlike its striped and brown relatives, a formidable hunter in its own right, not only a scavenger.

groups.name: Xenarthra
groups.fact: Sloths, anteaters, and armadillos, named for extra 'xenarthrous' joints between their lower spine vertebrae, found in no other mammal, which add rigidity to the lower back.

groups.name: Folivora
groups.fact: The sloths -- six living species split between two-toed and three-toed genera that are not each other's closest relatives, despite the shared name and lifestyle.

groups.name: Cingulata
groups.fact: Armadillos -- the only living mammals with a carapace of bony dermal plates covered in overlapping keratin scutes.

groups.name: Chlamyphoridae
groups.fact: Most living armadillo species, including the giant armadillo and the three-banded armadillos -- split from the long-nosed armadillos of Dasypodidae by molecular studies within the last two decades.

groups.name: Tolypeutes
groups.fact: Two living species of three-banded armadillo -- the only armadillos able to roll their whole body into a fully enclosed, armored ball; every other genus has too many plates to close all the way.

groups.name: Eulipotyphla
groups.fact: Hedgehogs, moles, and shrews -- small, mostly insect-eating mammals once lumped into a wider 'Insectivora' grouping since abandoned as not a true evolutionary group.

groups.name: Erinaceidae
groups.fact: Hedgehogs and their smooth-furred, spineless cousins the gymnures -- the only Eulipotyphlans that grow a coat of spines instead of ordinary fur.

groups.name: Erinaceus
groups.fact: Old World hedgehogs, including the European hedgehog -- spines that are hollow hairs stiffened with keratin, rolled into a closed ball by a pair of large muscles across the back.

groups.name: Herpestidae
groups.fact: The mongoose family -- over 30 species, in the same cat-like suborder Feliformes as the hyenas, though built more like a weasel than a cat.

groups.name: Suricata
groups.fact: A single living species, the meerkat -- Kalahari-dwelling and living in mobs where some members always stand sentry to watch for predators while the rest forage.
